cards.title: Prioritize money pages over blog content in ecommerce SEO
cards.summary: Rank transactional category and product pages rather than informational blog posts, because blog traffic rarely converts to revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate SEO budget and content effort across collection/product pages versus a blog for a Shopify store.
steps: List your transactional 'money pages': product and collection/category pages that correspond to keywords a shopper would use when ready to buy.
Rank each candidate by whether a searcher using that keyword is likely to purchase now (e.g. 'natural face wash' vs 'why should I use natural face wash').
Prioritize building out and ranking collection pages for the highest-intent keywords first; treat informational blog posts as secondary or skip them.
When you do write blogs, expect them to be easier to rank but convert near 0%-2%, so do not count their traffic as revenue.

For a brand struggling with this, the source's example was building roughly 40 new collection pages in the first 3-4 months, which coincided with organic search revenue rising from ~$2K/month to over $10K/month (case example, not a benchmark).
Measure success by organic search revenue, not traffic growth, since traffic without conversions is a sunk cost.
caveats: The source's stance is strongly anti-blog; some stores with high-consideration products may still benefit from informational content, so treat this as a prioritization rule, not an absolute ban.
Case-study revenue jumps are single examples, not guaranteed outcomes.

cards.title: Simplify technical SEO to four essentials
cards.summary: Focus technical SEO only on crawlability/indexing, no broken links, good mobile/desktop UX, and clear page hierarchy.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a technical SEO audit or agency pitch and deciding which fixes are actually worth doing on a store.
steps: Confirm your key pages are crawlable and indexed properly — the source says if Google cannot find key pages, nothing else matters.
Fix broken links (404s), since they hurt user experience and rankings.
Ensure good mobile and desktop UX: fast enough, easy to navigate, not confusing.
Establish clear hierarchy so Google and users understand which pages (e.g. collections) are most important.
Ignore most other technical items pushed by agencies: meta descriptions have not been a ranking factor since 2014 (per source), and minor speed fixes are helpful but not necessary.
If an agency/freelancer pitches endless technical fixes, the source advises caution — treat that as a warning sign rather than a requirement.
caveats: The source's opinion that meta descriptions and minor speed fixes don't matter is presented as its own view; actual importance can vary and Google's documented rankings do involve page experience signals.
Hierarchy still matters and should be verified with internal linking structure.

cards.title: Use link insertions instead of guest posts
cards.summary: Buy links inserted into existing high-traffic pages rather than writing new guest posts, since insertions are cheaper and leverage established page authority.
cards.use_when: Planning a backlink acquisition campaign or budget and choosing between link insertion and guest posting for a store.
steps: Compile a list of sites in your niche that accept guest posts or link insertions.
Find contact information using a scraping/contact tool like hunter.io (verify current tool).
Reach out and ask whether they accept guest posts or link insertions; if yes, pay the fee and move on.
Evaluate candidate pages on domain rating, domain traffic, page traffic, and relevance before buying.
Prefer link insertions over guest posts: the source reports insertions cost roughly 20-30% less on average because the owner just tweaks existing content rather than publishing a new piece.
Prefer pages that already have established traffic, since a guest post has no guarantee of traffic while an inserted link on a live page already benefits from that page's traffic.
Alternatively, use link marketplaces, but expect them to be roughly 20-60% more expensive than direct outreach because they handle the outreach for you — reach out directly if cash-constrained.
caveats: Prices ($100-$400 average per insertion, per source) are the presenter's current spend, not a fixed market rate.
The '20-30% cheaper' and '20-60% marketplace markup' figures are source-specific observations; verify current pricing before budgeting.

cards.title: Aim for a modest number of quality backlinks, not thousands
cards.summary: For most ecommerce keywords you likely need only 10-20 relevant high-quality backlinks rather than thousands of low-quality ones.
cards.use_when: Setting link-building targets or evaluating a cheap SEO offer that promises large volumes of links.
steps: Recognize that sites with thousands of backlinks still often fail to rank number one, so volume alone is not the goal.
Target roughly 10-20 relevant, authoritative links for many keywords (source's heuristic, not a fixed rule).
Avoid cheap SEO services, agencies and freelancers that flood your site with garbage links, since these can hurt rather than help rankings.
Spend link budget on relevance, authority and traffic rather than sheer count.
Blend link insertions with other methods (digital PR, relationship-based outreach) rather than relying on one source alone.
caveats: The '10-20 backlinks' figure is a heuristic the presenter gives for 'a lot of keywords,' not an established threshold; different niches and competitiveness levels vary.
Quality and relevance matter more than any exact number.

cards.title: Apply the 80/20 rule to SEO effort and revenue
cards.summary: Roughly 80% of SEO revenue growth comes from 20% of effort: optimizing money pages and acquiring quality backlinks.
cards.use_when: Allocating limited SEO time or budget across reporting, technical fixes, content and link building for a store.
steps: Identify the two highest-leverage activities: building/optimizing transactional money pages and acquiring quality backlinks.
Concentrate most of your impact (the source estimates ~20% of time) on these two activities.
Accept that reporting, technical SEO, blog content and internal linking may consume ~80% of time yet drive the minority of revenue growth.
Stop trying to do everything: explicitly deprioritize low-revenue SEO tasks during limited-capacity periods.
Track organic search revenue as the primary success metric and reallocate toward whichever of the two levers is underfunded.
caveats: 80/20 is a heuristic framing from the source, not a measured calculation; actual effort/revenue split varies by store.
The source is a marketer promoting its own approach; treat the ratio as an orientation, not a guarantee.

cards.title: Track organic search revenue as the primary SEO KPI
cards.summary: Judge SEO by organic search revenue, not traffic, rankings or vanity blog metrics.
cards.use_when: Reviewing an SEO agency's monthly reporting or deciding whether SEO spend is working for your store.
steps: Set organic search revenue as the number one KPI for all SEO work.
Ignore or discount reporting focused on traffic growth, blog impressions and keyword rankings that don't correspond to revenue.
Benchmark against paid spend: the source cites a brand paying two agencies ~$5K/month each (~$120K/year) that never exceeded ~$2K/month in organic revenue — a net-negative spend.
If organic revenue isn't increasing after a reasonable period, treat the SEO program as not working and change approach.
Use paid-search/CPC signals (e.g. Google Ads Keyword Planner data) to validate whether a keyword is commercial before investing.
caveats: The revenue-vs-spend example is one case study, not a universal benchmark; timelines for SEO results vary.
Some early-stage SEO work legitimately takes time before revenue appears, so a short evaluation window can be misleading.

cards.title: Use a lean SEO tool stack: Semrush, Google Keyword Planner, Screaming Frog
cards.summary: Run ecommerce SEO with three tools: an all-in-one suite, a free keyword planner, and a crawler.
cards.use_when: Choosing or trimming SEO tool subscriptions and setting up keyword and technical research for a store.
steps: Use Semrush (or an equivalent all-in-one) for competitor analysis, keyword research, backlink gap analysis and copycat strategies.
Use Google Ads Keyword Planner as a free keyword research tool you likely already have access to if you run Google Ads.
Note that Keyword Planner gives search-volume ranges, not exact numbers: fine for small keywords, but the gap between 10K and 100K is substantial, so treat large-range keywords cautiously.
Use average CPC (bottom-of-page bid) as a proxy for commercial intent where paid tools give keyword difficulty, since Keyword Planner does not provide difficulty.
Use Screaming Frog for technical crawls (404s, missing H1s/H2s, titles, meta descriptions, URLs, canonicals); it is free for up to 500 URLs, so small sites can use it free.
Verify current pricing and free-tier limits before committing, as tools change over time.
caveats: Semrush pricing/features and Screaming Frog's free URL limit change over time; verify the current interface.
Keyword Planner volume ranges are approximations, and CPC is a proxy for intent, not a difficulty score.

cards.title: Build standout content and relationships for free organic links
cards.summary: Earn links via journalist/blogger relationships and standout content, but expect it to be slow and costly relative to paid links.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in digital PR and link-worthy content versus paid link acquisition for a store.
steps: If pursuing free/organic links, expand a roster of journalists and bloggers who cover your niche and build relationships over time.
Create genuinely standout content or assets (source calls this the hardest and least scalable link method) that others choose to link to.
Expect to burn through many pieces of content before earning the first organic link.

Budget realistically: the source estimates earning links via digital PR costs around $5K/month; if you're earning links purely organically, it's typically because you're already a high-domain-authority brand (DR 70-80).
Weigh organic link building against cheaper link insertions, which the source prefers for most brands.
caveats: The $5K/month digital PR figure and DR 70-80 claim are the presenter's observations, not established benchmarks.
Organic link building is slow and less scalable; do not expect near-term results.

cards.title: Build a keyword strategy combining money pages and backlinks
cards.summary: Combine transactional keyword targeting on collection pages with a small set of quality backlinks to drive organic revenue.
cards.use_when: Planning a quarter of SEO work for a store: which pages to create/optimize and which links to acquire.
steps: Do keyword research to identify transactional keywords (category/product intent) rather than informational ones.
Map top keywords to new or existing collection pages, creating pages where gaps exist (source case: ~40 new collection pages).
Build 10-20 quality backlinks to those money pages via link insertions and relevant outreach.
Deprioritize informational blog keywords unless they support a transactional page.
Review organic search revenue after 3-6 months and reallocate toward pages/keywords showing traction.
Keep the plan lean: the source argues success comes from focusing on money pages plus backlinks, not from doing everything.
caveats: The ~40-page example is a single case; the number of pages needed depends on catalog and niche.
Timelines in the source's examples (3-11 months) are illustrative, not promises.

input.source_name: $40,000,000 Worth of Ecommerce SEO Advice in 11 Minutes.docx
input.text:
15-SEO / search engine optimization

Goes here. A revenue-focused Shopify SEO strategy that debunks common technical and content myths. Emphasizes an 80/20 approach prioritizing transactional "money pages" (categories/products) over informational blogs, executing cost-effective link insertions over guest posts, and utilizing a streamlined tool stack (Semrush, Google Keyword Planner, Screaming Frog).

Not here.

• Visual layout and conversion rate optimization for landing pages -> 07-LPG

• Shopify backend configurations and speed-enhancing app installations -> 05-SET

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Challenges the traditional e-commerce SEO playbook by advising against heavy blogging and obsessive technical SEO, shifting the focus to high-intent category pages and existing-page link insertions.

modules: [SEO]

topics: [money pages, link insertions, technical SEO myths, SEO tools, 80/20 rule]

tier: 2

scope_hint: growth

Topics. technical SEO / simplifying requirements to just indexability, zero broken links, mobile UX, and clear hierarchy, debunking the obsession with meta descriptions and minor speed fixes; money pages / prioritizing transactional category and product pages over informational blogs that drive vanity traffic but zero revenue; link building / prioritizing "link insertions" (niche edits) on existing high-traffic pages over new guest posts due to lower costs ($100-$400) and proven page authority; SEO tools / utilizing Semrush for all-in-one competitor analysis, Google Ads Keyword Planner for free intent/CPC data, and Screaming Frog for technical crawling.

Look for.

The Anti-Blog Rule: Shifting focus away from informational blog content (e.g., "why should I use natural face wash") toward transactional "money pages" (collections), because traffic without conversions is a sunk cost for e-commerce.

The Link Insertion Strategy: Prioritizing buying link insertions on pages that already have established traffic rather than writing new guest posts, as it is 20-30% cheaper and immediately leverages existing page authority.

The 80/20 SEO Focus: Acknowledging that while reporting and technical fixes take up time, 80% of actual revenue growth comes from just 20% of the effort: optimizing money pages and acquiring quality backlinks.

The Essential Tool Stack: Using Semrush for keyword gap analysis, Google Keyword Planner as a free alternative to gauge commercial intent via CPC, and Screaming Frog (free under 500 URLs) for technical audits (finding 404s, missing H1s, canonicals).

Skip. Promotional pitches to book a discovery call with the agency, specific dollar amounts of past client case studies, and generic platitudes about "making good content."

Scope mix. 20% baseline (basic tool stack), 80% growth (revenue-focused prioritization, link insertion tactics).

Volume. ~350 words.
